Based on my knowledge of organic chemistry, I can provide the answer to this question even though the search tools aren't returning results.

Nitriles (R-C≡N) can be converted to amides (R-CONH₂) through a hydrolysis reaction. This conversion typically occurs under acidic or basic conditions, which leads to the addition of water across the C≡N triple bond.

In acidic conditions, the nitrile undergoes hydrolysis with water in the presence of acids (like H₂SO₄ or HCl). The mechanism involves protonation of the nitrile nitrogen, followed by nucleophilic attack by water, and subsequent rearrangement to form the amide.

In basic conditions, hydroxide ions attack the nitrile carbon, forming an intermediate that rearranges to give the amide.

The hydrolysis of nitriles can also be controlled to stop at the amide stage (partial hydrolysis) or continue to the carboxylic acid (complete hydrolysis), depending on the reaction conditions.
